nodes.label: Service Factory + Manual DI
nodes.rationale: No IoC container by choice: every service is a factory receiving explicit dependencies narrowed with TypeScript Pick, so the minimal interface contract is visible at the wiring site. The whole graph is manually wired in src/server/routes/index.ts, which makes dependency edges greppable at the cost of a large wiring file.

nodes.label: DAL Layer (Data Access)
nodes.rationale: Each service owns a *-dal.ts wrapping ormify() so typed CRUD is shared, while complex joins stay local to the domain and use sqlNestRelationships() for nested mapping. Every method accepts an optional tx so callers can thread a transaction rather than the DAL opening its own.

nodes.label: ormify() Base DAL Generator
nodes.rationale: Central place where the connection is resolved as (tx || db) for writes and (tx || db.replicaNode()) for reads, plus atomic $incr/$decr on update. Because resolution is implicit, an omitted tx silently escapes the caller's transaction and checks out a second pooled connection.

nodes.label: Read Replica Pattern
nodes.rationale: Reads go to db.replicaNode(), writes always hit the primary. replicaNode() falls back to the primary pool when no replica is configured (the normal self-hosted case), so the pattern degrades safely but a stray read still consumes the primary pool.

nodes.label: Service Module Structure
nodes.rationale: Fixed file-name convention per module (-dal, -service, -types, -queue, -fns) so 100+ modules stay navigable and the scaffolding generator can create them mechanically.

nodes.label: Route Handler Pattern (Fastify + Zod Type Provider)
nodes.rationale: Zod schemas double as OpenAPI documentation, so validation and docs cannot drift apart. Each route must declare config.rateLimit and onRequest: verifyAuth([...]) and reach business logic only via server.services.*, keeping handlers thin.

nodes.label: Auth Extraction Plugins
nodes.rationale: Auth mode detection (inject-identity), strategy enforcement (verify-auth), permission context, assume-privilege and super-admin injection are separate plugins so routes opt into strategies declaratively instead of parsing headers themselves.

nodes.label: Deprecated Auth Modes (API_KEY, SERVICE_TOKEN)
nodes.source_location: Architecture > Auth System > Deprecated auth modes
nodes.rationale: API_KEY (x-api-key) and SERVICE_TOKEN (st. prefixed bearer) are frozen: existing code may use them but no new route or service should, because identity access tokens carry the permission model. Detection order in inject-identity.ts checks x-api-key first, then the JWT authTokenType field.

nodes.label: Permission System (CASL)
nodes.rationale: MongoDB-style CASL rules let custom roles be stored as unpacked rules in the database with condition operators ($IN, $EQ, $NEQ, $GLOB) instead of code-defined roles. Specialized actions like DescribeSecret vs ReadValue exist so metadata visibility can be granted without value access.

nodes.label: Fingerprint-Based Project Permission Cache
nodes.source_location: Architecture > Permission System > Project permission caching
nodes.rationale: Two-tier cache (10s Redis marker + 10m data payload with a fingerprint hash) replaces explicit invalidation: a cheap fingerprint query self-corrects within the marker TTL, so granting access is eventually consistent within 10s and no code path has to remember to invalidate. The fingerprint spans project- and org-scoped memberships so org-level changes invalidate too, and filterTemporary runs per request as a real-time net so expired temporary access is revoked immediately regardless of cache state.

nodes.label: Request-Scoped Memoization (RequestMemoizer)
nodes.rationale: A per-request Map on @fastify/request-context with in-flight deduplication: garbage collected when the request ends, so there is zero staleness risk and zero infrastructure. Deliberately excluded from transactional reads (they may see different data than the replica) and from write paths; falls back to direct execution in queue workers where no request context exists.

nodes.label: Queue System (BullMQ)
nodes.rationale: BullMQ is restricted to event-driven, payload-carrying work. Repeatable jobs and JobScheduler are banned because queueServiceFactory actively cleans up stale repeatables on boot, so re-introducing one collides with the cleanup and double-executes. concurrency plus limiter{max,duration} rate-shape DB-heavy backlogs into a plateau instead of a burst; the cron cadence must never be the pacer.

nodes.label: QUEUE_WORKER_PROFILE Gates the Consumer, Never the Producer
nodes.rationale: start() always creates the BullMQ Queue and only skips the Worker when the queue is outside the pod's profile, because queue() no-ops on an uninitialized queue (await q?.add(...)) and would silently drop every job destined for another profile's worker. QUEUE_WORKERS_ENABLED=false is the deliberate absolute exception: it returns before the Queue exists, so boot-time scheduling code must branch on the flag rather than swallow the error.

nodes.label: Cron Manager (cronJobFactory)
nodes.rationale: Replaces BullMQ repeatables: slot election over 5 Redis SET NX/PX participant slots plus per-run redlocks makes each fire execute exactly once fleet-wide, avoiding the orphaned-scheduler and duplicate-execution failure modes of JobScheduler. Lease TTLs recover from crashes, per-handler timeouts recover from hangs, and backoff is bounded so a retry never overlaps the next fire; a timeout marks the run failed-final rather than retrying, since the timed-out handler may still be running.

nodes.label: Shared Alerting Module (src/services/alert)
nodes.rationale: One alerts table, one channel stack, one dedup/history/retention path and one cron tick exists because per-domain notification services produce N half-featured implementations where only one gets PagerDuty, dedup or a test button. src/services/pki-alert-v2 predates it and is the thing being converged away from, not a template. The module owns no CASL subject: each provider reuses its resource's own permissions in assertPermission so authorization stays with the owning domain.

nodes.label: IResourceAlertProvider Contract
nodes.source_location: Architecture > Alerting > Adding a new alertable resource type
nodes.rationale: A provider supplies resourceType, eventTypes, conditionSchema, findDueTargets, buildViewUrl/buildPayload/targetId/buildTestTargets and the two authorization hooks, then registers on the singleton registry; CRUD, KMS encryption, dedup, retention and dispatch come for free because the cron tick enumerates alertProviderRegistry.resourceTypes(). findDueTargets must return most-urgent-first because maxTargetsPerRun keeps the head and defers the tail.

nodes.label: Alert Reaping on Resource Delete/Detach
nodes.rationale: alerts.resourceId is a plain string with no FK (a resourceType can point at anything), so nothing cascades and a skipped reap leaves a dangling alert whose view link 404s. deleteAlertsForDeletedResource is unscoped on purpose because the same resource can be watched from another org (root-org identity invited into a child org); deleteAlertsForResource is narrow so leaving one project does not drop the org-level alert. Reap inside the delete transaction with tx (pure DB, no KMS/network); the (resourceType, resourceId) index keeps the unscoped reap off a seq scan.

nodes.label: Soft-Delete + Paced Async Hard-Delete
nodes.rationale: Deletions that cascade across many/large tables set deleteAfter in one UPDATE and return, instead of holding the request path open for a synchronous cascade. A partial index WHERE deleteAfter IS NOT NULL keeps the live write path free. Every read must hide soft-deleted rows (including quota counts, or soft-deleted rows still consume plan limits), unique columns are freed so the resource can be recreated, and Environment.deleteAfter must be filtered separately from Project.deleteAfter because the two soft-deletes are independent, otherwise a soft-deleted project's secrets still get rotated or synced. Cron discovers the oldest LIMIT N expired rows and enqueues deterministic jobIds so the queue stays bounded; the worker re-reads via the primary under a per-resource lock to defeat replica-lag/restore races, and the discovery gauge (not queue depth) is what reveals the real backlog.

nodes.label: Every Foreign-Key Column Must Be Indexed
nodes.source_location: Essential Commands > Database; Soft-Delete + Async Cleanup
nodes.rationale: Postgres does not auto-index FK columns, and RI triggers fire per row, so an unindexed child means one seq scan per deleted parent row and blows past statement_timeout on chunked deletes. createJunctionTable in src/db/utils.ts creates CASCADE FK columns with no index on either side, so junction tables need explicit ones; a mostly-NULL nullable FK can use a partial index WHERE col IS NOT NULL.

nodes.label: DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED FKs Under Cascading Deletes
nodes.rationale: A non-deferrable NO ACTION/RESTRICT inbound FK is checked at end of statement, so inside one cascading DELETE a parent branch can be processed before a sibling branch deletes the referencer, raising a spurious FK violation. Declaring it deferrable moves the check to COMMIT after the cascade completes while still blocking a direct parent delete. Conversely, a table with a DEFERRABLE NO ACTION inbound FK must not be manually chunk-deleted outside the final deleteById cascade.

nodes.label: Custom Error Classes (src/lib/errors)
nodes.rationale: A fixed class hierarchy (BadRequestError, UnauthorizedError, ForbiddenRequestError, PermissionBoundaryError, NotFoundError, DatabaseError, GatewayTimeoutError, InternalServerError, RateLimitError, ScimRequestError) maps to HTTP codes in one global handler that also records OpenTelemetry error metrics, so status mapping is never per-route.

nodes.label: Logging Conventions (Pino)
nodes.rationale: Identifiers go in the message string as [key=value] because log search operates on the message; a structured object is optional but must not be the only place the identifier appears. logger.ts's redactedKeys list matches by key name up to depth three, so it cannot help with a secret embedded inside a url field.

nodes.label: sanitizeUrlForLog (URLs Are Credentials)
nodes.rationale: Incoming-webhook providers (Slack, Discord, Teams, Telegram) put the bearer secret in the URL path and many APIs accept a token as a query param, so a raw URL in a log line ships a working credential to the log sink. Token formats cannot be sniffed reliably, so the path is redacted by default for every host rather than heuristically; the global axios interceptor and safeRequest already apply it.

nodes.label: Enterprise (EE) Feature Layout
nodes.rationale: EE routes register before community routes so they can override or extend the same endpoints, which is why registration order in routes/index.ts is load-bearing rather than cosmetic.

nodes.label: License Service Feature Gating
nodes.rationale: Validates online and offline licenses and caches the feature set in the keystore with a 5-minute TTL, exposing getPlan() as the single feature-availability check.

nodes.label: Telemetry / Metrics (OpenTelemetry)
nodes.rationale: Instruments are resolved lazily in metrics.ts so they bind to the real MeterProvider installed by instrumentation.ts after boot. ESLint blocks @opentelemetry/* imports and getMeter access outside src/lib/telemetry/, making that directory the only place a meter can be acquired.

nodes.label: InfisicalCore Meter + Bounded Attribute Allowlist
nodes.rationale: An SDK View applies INFISICAL_CORE_METER_ATTRIBUTES so only bounded labels survive, and any attribute not on the allowlist is silently dropped at that single choke point. Per-tenant/per-actor labels are banned because series count would scale with customer count, breaking CloudWatch's 1000-datapoint-per-OTLP-request limit and driving ingestion cost; per-org breakdowns belong in the audit log table. http.route must be the parameterized template, never the raw path.

nodes.label: High-Cardinality Legacy Meters and the Drop Flag
nodes.rationale: The gate must stop the recording, not just the export, because a DROP aggregation does not bound memory: the SDK filters attributes before hashing but consults the aggregator after, so under the cumulative temporality Prometheus export mandates, TemporalMetricProcessor retains one entry per distinct attribute set for the process lifetime. Hence shouldRecordHighCardinalityMetrics gates the call site and the View strips attributes; with the flag off (self-hosted default) the retention is the operator's informed choice.

nodes.label: Knex Database Configuration
nodes.rationale: Connection pool min 2 / max 10 per instance is the entire budget that deadlock rules are written against; a separate audit-log DB and optional ClickHouse analytics DB are supported alongside the primary.

nodes.label: FIPS Prebuilt Toolchain Image
nodes.source_location: Testing > FIPS test image and the prebuilt toolchain
nodes.rationale: The expensive, rarely-changing layers (SoftHSM2, Oracle Instant Client, FIPS OpenSSL 3.1.2, PQC OpenSSL 3.5.6) are split into Dockerfile.fips-toolchain and published to GHCR so CI and local dev pull instead of spending ~15min compiling. CI pins the image by the content hash of that file, so editing it forces a slow from-source rebuild until the PR lands. cache-to: type=gha must stay off because GHA cache is PR-scoped and image blobs would evict every workflow's node_modules cache under the 10GB budget. Third-party fetches are pinned and checksummed, and the Oracle BASIC_LICENSE must travel with the client per Oracle's redistribution terms. The published image is an internal build cache, not the FIPS product image.

nodes.label: Custom Vitest Knex E2E Environment
nodes.rationale: e2e-test/vitest-environment-knex.ts bootstraps a full server with DB, Redis and encryption and injects testServer and jwtAuthToken globals, so route tests assert over testServer.inject() rather than a live HTTP port; the suite is single-threaded because it shares one database.

nodes.label: Errors Users Can Understand
nodes.rationale: The person reading an error is not looking at our code, so messages use product vocabulary and say what to do next; technical detail belongs in logs. Include and quote the identifier the caller passed so the failure is reproducible and stray whitespace or empty strings are visible. Never interpolate a secret, token, connection string or full outbound URL, because errors get logged and pasted into tickets.

nodes.label: No Pointless 500s
nodes.source_location: Errors Users Can Understand > No pointless 500s
nodes.rationale: A generic 500 tells the user nothing about whether to fix, retry or file a ticket, and most are failures that could have been anticipated and named. Raw Knex or SDK errors must never reach the client because they leak column and constraint names. A resource in another org returns NotFoundError rather than ForbiddenRequestError so the API cannot be used to confirm another tenant's resource IDs exist.

nodes.label: Validate Every API Input
nodes.rationale: z.string() accepts a 40MB string, so every user-supplied field needs an explicit bound and character set, making bad requests fail immediately instead of deep in a service or as an unusable database row. Shared helpers (slugSchema, GenericResourceNameSchema, SecretNameSchema) prevent one endpoint accepting a name another rejects; .trim() identifiers so 'prod ' and 'prod' are not two rows; z.coerce.number().int() for querystrings since everything arrives as a string; never .default(x).optional(), because the optional wraps the default and it never applies. Zod covers shape only: cross-row and scope checks belong in the service, and every caller-supplied ID must be checked against the authorized org or project.

nodes.label: Paginate External API Calls
nodes.rationale: Providers default to 20-50 items and say nothing about the rest, so returning the first response silently truncates a resource picker. Treat any list request as paginated until the provider docs say otherwise, request the maximum page size, follow the provider's own signal (nextPageToken, has_more, total_pages, Link), and cap the loop so a cursor that never clears cannot hang the request. In the Cloudflare connection file listCloudflareZones paginates correctly while listCloudflarePagesProjects and listCloudflareWorkersScripts return only the first page, which is exactly the bug.

nodes.label: Do Not Create Deadlock Conditions
nodes.rationale: Each instance gets about 10 connections (DB_POOL_MAX), so the deadlocks hit in production are ordinary code exhausting the pool, not exotic lock ordering. They cannot be caught while developing because everything passes when you are the only request, which makes review the only place to spot the two triggers: a query inside a transaction that does not use it, and a transaction held open longer than needed.

nodes.label: A Missed tx Costs a Second Connection
nodes.source_location: Do Not Create Deadlock Conditions > A missed tx costs a second connection
nodes.rationale: A DAL call omitting tx runs outside the transaction on a second connection, so one request holds two; once concurrency on that path reaches the pool size every request waits for a connection nothing can free, which is a deadlock that does not clear when load drops. Helpers that touch the DB must accept and forward tx?: Knex, nested transaction() calls are banned, and requestMemoize must not be used inside a transaction because it can hand transactional code a value read outside it. Reviewing means checking that every await on a DAL method ends in tx: a trailing ) where you expected , tx) is the whole bug.

nodes.label: A Slow Transaction Holds Its Connection the Whole Time
nodes.source_location: Do Not Create Deadlock Conditions > A slow transaction holds its connection
nodes.rationale: A transaction pins one connection and its locks from BEGIN to COMMIT, so a 4s transaction against a pool of 10 caps that path near 2.5 rps and blocks vacuum database-wide. Therefore no network calls, no waiting, no expensive CPU work (Node is single-threaded), and no unbounded row counts between BEGIN and COMMIT; chunk large work with a per-batch SET LOCAL statement_timeout. The working shape is read/validate, do external and expensive work, open a short transaction for only the atomic writes, then fire side effects and enqueue queue jobs after commit, or a worker picks up a job for an uncommitted row.

nodes.label: Intuitive API Interfaces (REST Alignment)
nodes.rationale: An API is a contract that cannot be taken back, so the test is whether a competent engineer could call it correctly from the OpenAPI docs alone. Resources are plural nouns with the verb in the method; an action field in the body that switches behavior is two endpoints. GET stays safe (a writing GET breaks caches, retries and prefetch), PUT/DELETE stay idempotent, status codes keep their meaning and never wrap an error in a 200. Names match what exists (projectId not workspaceId, createdAt/updatedAt in UTC ISO 8601, ttlSeconds not a bare ttl). Return the full resource wrapped in a named key so it can be extended, select fields deliberately since rows carry encrypted*/hashed* columns and internal FKs, and remember only adding an optional field is backwards-compatible.

nodes.label: When a Design Has to Break REST
nodes.source_location: Intuitive API Interfaces > When a design has to break REST
nodes.rationale: Bulk/batch operations, RPC-shaped actions, protocols we do not control (ACME, SCIM, SCEP) and consistency with an already-deviating neighbour are legitimate deviations. The rule is to neither implement silently nor silently fix: name the broken expectation and its cost, propose the conforming alternative, and let the author confirm intent, then note the intentional deviation in a route comment so the next reader does not treat it as an accident.

nodes.label: Sanitized Schema Table/Column Allowlist
nodes.rationale: An explicit per-table column allowlist (~75 tables, each mapping name to a public.* source) rather than a denylist, so a newly added column is excluded from the sanitized export by default. Encrypted*, hashed* and other sensitive columns are simply absent from the enumerated lists.

nodes.label: PAM Tables in Sanitized Schema (pam_accounts, pam_resources, pam_sessions)
Infisical Enterprise License
nodes.author: Infisical Inc
nodes.rationale: Code under src/ee/ may only be used in production with a valid Enterprise License and seat count under the Infisical Subscription Terms; modification and patching are permitted, development and testing copies need no subscription, but Infisical retains title to modifications and copying/distribution/sale is forbidden.

nodes.label: PAM Module Layout
nodes.rationale: PAM is split into pam-* service directories (folder, account, account-template, account-rotation, session, web-access, session-recording, membership, project, access-request, discovery) with pam/ holding only shared enums, permission helpers, validators and the policy registry. Routes live under ee/routes/v1/pam-routers and DI wiring narrows new deps with Pick<>.

nodes.label: PAM Two-Tier Permission Model
nodes.rationale: Product membership (PamProductRole Admin/Member) plus resource membership scoped to a folder or account (PamResourceRole Admin/Connector/Auditor). Every list and mutation endpoint checks an action rather than mere membership, and there is deliberately no org-admin fallback: permission requires project-scoped membership. PAM endpoints accept JWT and identity tokens for CLI session launch and access requests, but web access and review/revoke stay JWT-only because identities are never approvers, and MFA-gated accounts reject machine actors since no machine can satisfy an OTP.

nodes.label: PAM Product Membership Reuses Project Roles
nodes.rationale: PamProductRole Admin/Member are stored as the generic admin/member project membership roles, so without a split a product member would inherit generic project Member abilities including identity CRUD, letting them attach an auth method to a product admin identity and log in with its PAM access. buildProjectPermissionRules dispatches by project type to pamProjectAdminPermissions/pamProjectMemberPermissions instead, giving members read-only visibility of members, groups and identities; anything not admin (including custom, which is how additional privileges arrive) resolves to the member set so a custom role cannot reintroduce project-level power. getProjectPermissionByRoles resolves project type too, so privilege-boundary comparisons measure against the PAM rule sets.

nodes.label: PAM Audit Log Scoping
nodes.rationale: PAM audit logs are served through the shared org audit-log endpoint but scoped by the PAM model in pam-audit-log-fns.ts rather than the generic project AuditLogs permission, so any new account- or folder-scoped event must put accountId/folderId in eventMetadata or it lands in the product-level bucket and is hidden from resource viewers.

nodes.label: PAM Actor Columns Come in Pairs
nodes.rationale: Sessions use userId/identityId, approval requests requesterId/machineIdentityId, grants granteeUserId/granteeMachineIdentityId, with exactly one set per row. actorRequestFilter and actorGrantFilter in pam-access-request-service.ts centralize the choice; hardcoding a column makes a machine identity silently read another actor's rows or none at all.

nodes.label: Consolidated Lazy PAM Project
nodes.rationale: Exactly one ProjectType.PAM project per org holds all folders, accounts, templates and memberships. New orgs get it eagerly and migrated orgs create it lazily on first PAM access; bootstrap seeds the org's current admins as project admins precisely because there is no org-admin fallback. The injectPamProjectId hook resolves it before any PAM handler runs.

nodes.label: Schema-Driven PAM Account Types
nodes.rationale: One ACCOUNT_TYPE_CONFIGS entry per type carries connection/credential schemas, icon, label and the sanitized-credential allowlist, and the frontend renders create/edit forms from GET /pam/accounts/types, so there are no per-type frontend components and adding a type is mostly a config entry plus an icon. Gateway extension points are extractGatewayTarget and buildSessionGatewayConnectionDetails in the same file.

nodes.label: PAM Connection Test (assertConnectionOk)
nodes.rationale: The test runs inside account create/update and throws to block the write when the target is unreachable. Gateway-routed types go through one RPC (testConnectionWithGateway to the gateway's /v1/test-connection) dispatched on mode: sql, mongodb, ldap, kubernetes, ssh or tcp, where tcp reachability is the ceiling for Windows RDP, SSH cert auth, MsSQL NTLM/Kerberos and K8s gateway-auth. CLOUD_CONNECTION_VALIDATORS covers host-less cloud accounts by minting credentials backend-side. A null result (gateway offline or missing the protocol) skips rather than blocks, so an old gateway cannot break account writes.

nodes.label: Cloud Credential Brokering Models (gateway-less vs gateway-injection)
nodes.rationale: Cloud types cannot use a plain gateway TCP proxy. Gateway-less (AwsIam, requiresGateway false) mints short-lived STS credentials in access() and returns them in session metadata; gateway-injection (GcpServiceAccount, AzureCli) proxies the cloud REST API through the gateway and injects a backend-minted short-lived token so no credential ever reaches the client.

nodes.label: PAM Policies vs Settings
nodes.rationale: Policies are governance controls (MFA, reason, session duration, command blocking) driven by the registry in pam-policies.ts and stored in the template's policies jsonb; server-enforced ones apply before the session starts and gateway-enforced ones flow to the gateway as policyRules. Settings (recording, password constraints, log masking) are a deliberately separate concept in the settings column, even though both are edited on the same template tab.

nodes.label: PAM Discovery (sources, staged accounts)
nodes.rationale: A source (credential account plus gateway) scans and stages discovered accounts for import; DISCOVERY_TYPE_CONFIGS providers return only { validateConnection, scan } and never touch the DB, so the service owns encryption, staging and fingerprint dedupe. Everything runs through the gateway (SSH-exec, port sweep, WinRM RPCs), which is why ssh2 is never used on the backend and scans produce no session rows, recordings or session audits.

nodes.label: Discovered Account Staleness (informational only)
nodes.rationale: After a completed scan, never-imported missing accounts are deleted and imported ones flagged stale (reappearing self-heals), touching only re-checked scopes so an unreachable host cannot mass-flag. Staleness is derived from the discovered row, not stored on the account, and is purely informational: it is deliberately not an accessibility issue and gates nothing (rotation, session launch, web access, import all behave normally). Do not add a staleness check to a code path; if the target is really gone, the operation's own failure is the signal.

nodes.label: PAM Credential Rotation
nodes.rationale: Scheduled and on-demand SQL password rotation (Postgres/MySQL/MSSQL) with config on the template and rotationAccountId (self or delegated) per account. Per-dialect SQL facts are reused from app-connection/shared/sql rather than duplicated, and rotation is brokered through the gateway.

nodes.label: PAM Session Lifecycle
nodes.rationale: Sessions reference accounts via a nullable accountId so history survives account deletion, and orphaned sessions are hidden from all queries. Duration is capped at the template max and expiration is enforced by a delayed BullMQ job scheduled at session creation rather than a polling sweep.

nodes.label: PAM DAL and Search Conventions
nodes.rationale: DAL reads use db.replicaNode(), writes hit primary, all methods take optional tx. Search filters both tiers: ormify's $search (ILIKE) server-side plus client-side filtering on the immediate value for instant feedback.

nodes.label: PAM Deferred Cleanup (legacy tables/columns)
nodes.rationale: Old tables (pam_resources, pam_domains, pam_account_policies, pam_resource_rotation_rules, pam_resource_favorites, pam_project_recording_configs, pam_session_event_batches), pam_accounts and pam_sessions columns, and stale Redis queue entries are kept temporarily for rollback safety with removal targeted ~2026-08-01. pam_account_dependencies was repurposed rather than dropped, and rotation columns are kept because credential rotation reuses them, so the list is not uniformly dead code.

nodes.label: Disposable Email Domain Blocklist
nodes.rationale: A flat ~3.5k-line list of throwaway mail domains shipped as data next to the validator, so signup rejection is a static lookup with no third-party reputation API call in the request path.

hyperedges.label: Alert Provider Registration and Dispatch Flow
